reader_summary.headline: Tony James shares how he built Blackstone and backed Costco.
reader_summary.overview: Tony James discusses growing a small investment bank into a massive firm. He explains his strategy for buying companies, his long partnership with Costco, and his leadership lessons from Charlie Munger. He also details how he transformed Blackstone's culture and prepared for its public listing.

key_points.text: James turned a struggling bank into a top player by focusing on high-yield debt trading for twelve years.
key_points.evidence_quote: We accounted for all of 40% of Wall trading volume in high yield for 12 years.

key_points.text: James prioritized succession planning by grooming John Gray to take over while the company was still growing.
key_points.evidence_quote: But succession planning was one of them. I had to nail that. And that's a process.

key_points.text: Costco succeeds by constantly lowering prices for customers rather than raising them to increase short-term profits.

key_points.text: Tony James convinced Steve Schwarzman to take a risky deal by personally guaranteeing the interest payments if the deal failed.
key_points.evidence_quote: Steve said, well, are you want to put your money on your own personal money on the line? And I said, yes.

notes: David Haber speaks with Tony James about building enduring firms across multiple eras of finance. From joining DLJ when it was a subscale firm to helping grow Blackstone into one of the largest asset managers in the world, James reflects on the decisions, structures, and cultural principles that enabled long-term success. They discuss the origins of leveraged buyouts, the evolution of private markets, and how identifying structural opportunities early can create lasting competitive advantage. James also shares lessons from backing companies like Costco, where culture, customer focus, and long-term thinking drove exceptional outcomes. The conversation covers leadership, talent development, and the challenges of scaling organizations while maintaining performance. James also reflects on succession, firm-building, and why culture, incentives, and alignment ultimately determine whether an organization compounds or stagnates.
